selection: biased information reasons that cause costs
description: The most relevant reasons why biased information causes costs, each linked to biased information with 'can cause' and quantified by the studies that report it for the world and per country: the overstated efficacy of drugs caused by the selective publication of the antidepressant trials (Turner et al. 2008) and by the industry sponsorship of the drug and device studies (Lundh et al. 2017); the research waste caused by the trials that are never published (Turner et al. 2008, Glasziou & Chalmers); the cost overrun of the transport infrastructure projects caused by the strategic misrepresentation of the cost estimates (Flyvbjerg, Holm & Buhl 2002); the change of the vote share caused by the slanted news of Fox News (DellaVigna & Kaplan 2007, Martin & Yurukoglu 2017); the decline of the COVID-19 vaccination intent caused by misinformation (Loomba et al. 2021); the traffic deaths caused by the misjudged risk of flying after 11 September 2001 (Gigerenzer 2006); and the return loss of the retirement savers caused by conflicted investment advice (Council of Economic Advisers 2015). The assumed share of the decisions taken on biased information and its solution, the Delphi method, are stated in problem_biased_information.json instead, because they are the row of the global problem ranking of the start page. The total research waste and the cost of the Tamiflu stockpile of the United Kingdom are added as context; these values are not attributed to biased information by their sources, because the research waste also includes the design flaws and the stockpile was bought while the full trial data were not available but without a statement that the money was lost, so they do not carry a '<reason> due to biased information' triple. Every number is taken from the named source as reported; a country that a study does not report is left out and never estimated. A share is stored as the decimal ratio, a loss as a positive number and a change with its sign. Each study has its own sample and metric, so numbers of different studies are not comparable without reading the source description. Every amount of money is stated in euro: the US dollar figure of the source is converted with the ECB 2023 annual average of 1.0813 USD per EUR (the value of GDP.json) whatever the price base year of the source, and the British pound figure with the ECB 2023 annual average of 0.86979 GBP per EUR, and the source figure is kept in the description of the value. A value of a reason carries the triple '<reason> due to biased information' and not the phrase 'biased information' itself, because a value that names a global problem directly is a row of the global problem ranking of the start page, where only the potential loss and the solution of a problem belong.

sources.name: Turner et al. (2008)
sources.description: Turner, E. H., Matthews, A. M., Linardatos, E., Tell, R. A., Rosenthal, R. (2008): Selective Publication of Antidepressant Trials and Its Influence on Apparent Efficacy. New England Journal of Medicine 358(3), 252-260. FDA reviews of 74 registered studies of 12 antidepressants with 12'564 patients: 31 percent of the studies, with 3'449 participants, were not published; according to the published literature 94 percent of the trials were positive, according to the FDA analysis 51 percent; the effect size of the published literature was 32 percent higher overall than the one of the full FDA data, 11 to 69 percent for the individual drugs.

sources.name: Lundh et al. (2017) Industry sponsorship and research outcome
sources.description: Lundh, A., Lexchin, J., Mintzes, B., Schroll, J. B., Bero, L. (2017): Industry sponsorship and research outcome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2017, MR000033. 75 papers: industry sponsored drug and device studies more often had favorable efficacy results, risk ratio 1.27 (95 percent CI 1.17 to 1.37, 25 papers, moderate quality evidence), and more often favorable conclusions, risk ratio 1.34 (95 percent CI 1.19 to 1.51, 29 papers, low quality evidence), than non-industry sponsored studies; an industry bias that cannot be explained by the standard risk of bias assessments.

sources.name: Glasziou & Chalmers (2016) Is 85% of health research really wasted
sources.description: Glasziou, P., Chalmers, I. (2016): Is 85% of health research really 'wasted'? The BMJ Opinion blog, 14 January 2016, explaining the estimate of their 2009 Lancet paper 'Avoidable waste in the production and reporting of research evidence': about 50 percent of the registered clinical trials are never published in full; half of the studies are published, half of those are reported well enough to use and half of those have no avoidable design flaws, so 87.5 out of 100 are wasted, rounded down to 85 percent; with USD 200 billion per year spent globally on health and medical research this implies an annual waste of USD 170 billion.

sources.name: Flyvbjerg, Holm & Buhl (2002)
sources.description: Flyvbjerg, B., Holm, M. S., Buhl, S. (2002): Underestimating Costs in Public Works Projects: Error or Lie? Journal of the American Planning Association 68(3), 279-295. 258 transport infrastructure projects worth USD 90 billion in Europe, North America and other geographical areas (10 developing nations plus Japan): the costs are underestimated in almost 9 out of 10 projects, the likelihood of actual costs larger than estimated is 86 percent; actual costs are on average 28 percent higher than estimated (sd 39), 44.7 percent for rail, 33.8 percent for fixed links (bridges and tunnels) and 20.4 percent for roads; the underestimation cannot be explained by error and is best explained by strategic misrepresentation, that is, lying.

sources.name: DellaVigna & Kaplan (2007) The Fox News Effect
sources.description: DellaVigna, S., Kaplan, E. (2007): The Fox News Effect: Media Bias and Voting. Quarterly Journal of Economics 122(3), 1187-1234. 9'256 towns of the United States, of which 20 percent got Fox News in their cable programming between October 1996 and November 2000: the Republicans gained 0.4 to 0.7 percentage points of the vote share in the presidential elections in the towns that broadcast Fox News; Fox News convinced 3 to 28 percent of its viewers to vote Republican, depending on the audience measure.

sources.name: Martin & Yurukoglu (2017) Bias in Cable News
sources.description: Martin, G. J., Yurukoglu, A. (2017): Bias in Cable News: Persuasion and Polarization. American Economic Review 107(9), 2565-2599. Using the cable channel positions as exogenous shifters of the viewership: removing Fox News from the cable television would have reduced the Republican presidential vote share by 0.46 percentage points in 2000, 3.59 percentage points in 2004 and 6.34 percentage points in 2008, driven by the increasing viewership and the increasingly conservative slant; figures as stated in the author version of 5 April 2017.

sources.name: Loomba et al. (2021) COVID-19 vaccine misinformation
sources.description: Loomba, S., de Figueiredo, A., Piatek, S. J., de Graaf, K., Larson, H. J. (2021): Measuring the impact of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on vaccination intent in the UK and USA. Nature Human Behaviour 5, 337-348. Randomized controlled trial of September 2020: relative to factual information, recent misinformation induced a decline in the vaccination intent of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.

sources.name: Gigerenzer (2006) Out of the frying pan into the fire
sources.description: Gigerenzer, G. (2006): Out of the frying pan into the fire: behavioral reactions to terrorist attacks. Risk Analysis 26(2), 347-351. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 the Americans reduced their air travel and drove instead; in the following year the fatal highway crashes exceeded the baseline of the previous years in each month; an estimated 1'500 Americans died on the road in the attempt to avoid the fate of the passengers of the four fatal flights, attributed to the fear of the dread risk.

sources.name: CEA (2015) The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings
sources.description: Council of Economic Advisers, Furman, J., Stevenson, B. (2015): The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings, February 2015. Savers receiving conflicted advice earn returns roughly 1 percentage point lower each year; an estimated USD 1.7 trillion of the IRA assets are invested in products that generate conflicts of interest, so the aggregate annual cost of the conflicted advice is about USD 17 billion each year.

sources.name: NAO (2013) Access to clinical trial information and the stockpiling of Tamiflu
sources.description: National Audit Office (2013): Access to clinical trial information and the stockpiling of Tamiflu. Memorandum for the Committee of Public Accounts, HC 125, Session 2013-14, 21 May 2013. Between 2006-07 and 2012-13 the Department of Health purchased nearly 40 million units of Tamiflu at a cost of GBP 424 million at 2011-12 prices; a key concern was that without full clinical trial information public money could be spent on ineffective medicines; 6.5 million units were written off at a cost of GBP 74 million because of poor record keeping.
